name: Erik Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Erik. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to tech companies, employers or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you describe a normal working week?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the assistant engineer at a small recording studio above a carpet shop, and I play keys on whatever session needs them. Most days it's setting up microphones for local bands, editing podcasts and cleaning up vocal takes. Once a month I DJ at a bar called the Signal Box, and I make beats at night that I sell online for about 30 pounds each.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a nervous band hears their first proper mix played back loud. I use AI tools every day, for splitting songs into parts, cleaning noise, tagging files. The hard part is that I'm the junior, my mixes still need my boss Dev to fix them, and the pay is low. I share a flat with a mate and I've got about two weeks of rent saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you, AI is a good set of tools and that's all it is. I'd post a quick video of my podcast cleanup workflow, because people always ask. Most engineers I know would shrug.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me. The studio's busy with podcasts and local bands, and Dev just gave me an extra day. My worry is the usual one: low pay and nothing in the bank if the studio has a quiet month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do and use the tools to get faster, so I can take on more podcast edits. I'd raise my beat prices from 30 to 40 pounds. I'd try to put aside 80 pounds a month so I'm not always two weeks from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay. A bit of the usual money worry, but the job feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a quiet month is the risk. What happened the last time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last February two bands cancelled, the studio cut me to three days, and I borrowed 200 pounds from my sister to cover the rent. I paid her back in April, but I didn't like asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at the studio you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really in this picture. Dev's been doing it twenty years and the place has regulars. If anything, the tools make us cheaper than the big studios in the city.

say: AI is a good **set of tools**, and that's all it is.
He'd post a video of his **podcast cleanup** workflow.
think: The **studio is busy** and he's just been given an extra day.
His worry is **low pay** and no savings for a quiet month.
do: Use AI to take on **more podcast edits**.
S0.quote: Last February two bands cancelled, the studio cut me to three days, and I borrowed 200 pounds from my sister to cover the rent.
fieldNote: His job feels **secure for now**; the risk is a quiet month.
He already uses AI **every day** and sees it as speed.
Borrowing from his **sister** shows how thin the cushion is.

steps.text: Use AI cleanup tools to take on more podcast edits
Raise online beat prices from 30 to 40 pounds
Save 80 pounds a month into a separate account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left, but nicely. I'd post about how small studios can use AI to be cheaper and faster. I'd also say the human ear still matters for the final mix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, a lot of my job is exactly what this picture says AI takes. Editing podcasts, cleaning vocals, tagging files: software will do it in seconds. If clients can upload to an app, Dev doesn't need a junior, he needs someone who can sit with a band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who runs the AI side of the studio, so Dev keeps me for that. I'd shift towards live work, sound for gigs and events, which is still hands-on. I'd buy a small second-hand PA system, about 600 pounds paid over six months, and hire it out with me for parties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Edgy, but kind of excited. It's scary and it's an opening at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're planning to buy gear with two weeks of rent saved. Isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it is. But a PA that earns 150 pounds a party pays for itself in four parties. I'd only buy it once I had three bookings lined up, so I'm not paying for a box in my bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame, if anyone, for that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody, really. Tools get better, that's what tools do. I'd just want the rules to be clear about who owns the songs the AI learned from, because that's fair to the bands we record.

Small studios can use AI to be **cheaper and faster**.
The **human ear** still matters for the final mix.

Shift towards **live sound** for gigs and events.
Buy a **second-hand PA** for about 600 pounds once three bookings are in.
feel: **Edgy** but **excited**; scary and an opening at once.
S1.quote: A PA that earns 150 pounds a party pays for itself in four parties.
fieldNote: He expects his **junior role** to shrink, so he repositions fast.
He takes **measured risks**: gear only after three bookings.
He **blames nobody** and wants clear rules on song ownership.

steps.text: Run the studio's AI editing tools so Dev keeps him
Buy a second-hand PA once three party bookings are in
Offer live sound for local gigs and events

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to think hard about how people get paid when AI does the work. I'd be fairly level about it online, I'm not one for doom posts. With friends I'd talk about what still needs a person in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, by 2028 the studio side of my job is gone, because recording, editing, mixing and mastering are all screen work. What's left is live: carrying speakers, plugging in cables, reading a room at a party. That's maybe three more years until the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on live events straight away: sound for weddings, parties and the Signal Box, with my own PA. I'd ask Dev if I can use the studio van at weekends. I'd also learn electrical basics, because event power and rigging are hands-on and paid well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaken, but moving. I'd feel it more at night than in the day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With robots about three years behind the thinking AI, how long do you think live sound lasts for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years, maybe five if people still want a person at a party. After that I don't know. I'd use those years to save hard and learn a trade like electrician, because that's hands-on but also needs thinking on the spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, my boss. He's 48 and the studio is his whole thing. If AI does the mixing, he's the one with a lease and nothing coming in. I'd try to bring him on the live jobs with me.

say: We need to think about **how people get paid** when AI does the work.
think: By 2028 the **studio side** of his job is gone; it's all screen work.
Live sound is hands-on and lasts until **robots**, maybe three years.
do: Go **all in** on live events with his own PA.

Learn **electrical basics** for event power and rigging.
feel: **Shaken but moving**; it hits harder at night.
S2.quote: By 2028 the studio side of my job is gone, because recording, editing, mixing and mastering are all screen work.
fieldNote: He clearly maps his job into **screen work** and **hands-on** work.
He plans to use the **robot gap** to save and train as an electrician.
He worries for his **boss**, not just himself.

steps.text: Book weddings and parties as a live sound engineer
Start an evening electrical basics course
Save hard from live gigs before robots arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is short but workable, so start now. I'd post tips for engineers moving into live work. I'd keep it practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years suits me. I can grow the live side while the studio still pays. By 2031 I want to be the go-to live sound guy in town, with an electrical qualification behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy the PA once I've got bookings, and run sound at ten events. I'd start the electrician apprenticeship enquiries, because those have waiting lists. I'd use AI to run my bookings, quotes and invoices so I spend my time on the jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Focused. A bit nervous about money, but it feels like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the studio still pays for a while. How long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two or three years, getting thinner. Podcast clients go first, because those are easy for AI, but bands like hanging out in a real room. They'll hang on longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your sister about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm not borrowing again, that's the point of it. She'd laugh, because she's heard that before. But this time I'd have the PA and a list of bookings to show her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for everyone to plan, so let's not waste it. I'd tell younger engineers to learn live sound and a trade alongside the studio work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is comfortable for me. I could build a proper live sound business and still do studio sessions for years. I'd be 37 when AGI lands, with my own kit and clients.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the studio job and grow live sound on weekends. I'd buy the PA this year and maybe a second set of speakers next year. I'd save 100 pounds a month and build up three months' rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Some nerves, but they're about money, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything you'd do with your beats?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep selling them while they sell. AI will make beats free long before 2036, so my beats are pocket money now, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in this picture for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting comfortable. Ten years sounds like forever, and I could drift. I'd set myself targets each year so I don't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd only have the robot gap to change trades, and I've got no money to train with. What would help is paid apprenticeships for people moving from screen work into hands-on trades, and a small loan scheme for kit like a PA.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people already use AI for. I use AI every day, and it makes me better at my job right now. That's why it's weird to picture it taking the job.

headlineQuote: I use AI every day, and it makes me better at my job right now. That's why it's weird to picture it taking the job.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old assistant engineer** at a small studio who DJs monthly and sells beats.
He uses **AI daily** and has about two weeks of rent saved after once borrowing from his sister.
He feels okay in AI Plateau but sees his **screen work** as exposed in every other picture.
His plan is **live sound** with his own PA, then an electrician apprenticeship.
He **blames nobody** and wants clear rules on who owns the songs AI learned from.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with only the robot gap to switch trades and no money.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** for people moving from screen work to trades.
A small **loan scheme** for kit like a PA.
